cover.title: 50 Most Asked API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: What's Inside
cover.tagline: 12 themed pages from REST basics to real-world design, each answer a short reply, key points and a visual. For backend and SDE interview prep.

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its constraints?
a_bullets: A ==REST API== exposes resources as URLs and manipulates them with standard HTTP methods. It follows six architectural constraints.
Resources are nouns: `/users/42`, not `/getUser`
Representations are usually JSON, sent over HTTP
**Stateless**, cacheable, uniform interface are the core ones
Code on demand is the only optional constraint

blocks.q: Q2. What is the difference between REST and SOAP?
a_bullets: REST is an ==architectural style== over plain HTTP. SOAP is a strict ==protocol== with an XML envelope.
REST: lightweight, JSON, cache-friendly, flexible
SOAP: XML only, contract-first through a **WSDL**
SOAP has built-in WS-Security and WS-AtomicTransaction
Choose SOAP for banks and legacy enterprise integrations

blocks.q: Q3. What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC?
a_bullets: All three expose services. They differ in ==shape of the call== and the wire format.
REST: many URLs, fixed responses, easy HTTP caching
GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields, avoids over-fetching
gRPC: Protobuf over HTTP/2, fast, strongly typed, streaming
Public API: REST. Mobile BFF: GraphQL. Microservices: gRPC

blocks.q: Q4. What does stateless mean in REST and why does it matter?
a_bullets: The server keeps ==no client session== between requests. Every request carries all the context needed, such as a token.
Any server instance can answer any request
Horizontal scaling is easy: just add servers behind a load balancer
Failures are simple: no session to lose or replicate
Cost: the token or context is sent on every call

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say stateless first: it explains REST scaling, caching and token auth.

blocks.q: Q5. What are the parts of an HTTP request and response?
a_bullets: A request has a ==start line==, headers and an optional body. A response has a status line, headers and a body.
Request line: method + path + HTTP version
Headers: metadata like `Content-Type` and `Authorization`
Body: payload, used by POST, PUT and PATCH
Response status line: version + code + reason, e.g. `201 Created`

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Walk it in order: line, headers, blank line, body. Mention `Location` on 201.

blocks.q: Q6. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a_bullets: ==PUT== replaces the whole resource with the body. ==PATCH== changes only the fields you send.
PUT with a missing field resets it to null or default
PATCH body is small: only the changed fields
PUT is **idempotent**; PATCH is not guaranteed

blocks.q: Q7. What is the difference between safe and idempotent HTTP methods?
a_bullets: A ==safe== method never changes server state. An ==idempotent== method leaves the same end state however many times you repeat it.
Every safe method is idempotent, but not the reverse
PUT and DELETE are idempotent: a 2nd DELETE may return 404, state is the same
POST is **neither**: a retry can double-charge (see page 10)

blocks.q: Q8. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: ==401== means the server doesn't know who you are. ==403== means it knows you, but you aren't allowed.
401 = authentication failed: no token, expired or bad
403 = authorization failed: valid user, wrong role or scope
A fresh login fixes 401, **never** 403

blocks.q: Q9. When do you return 400, 404, 409, 422 and 429?
a_bullets: Pick the code by what went wrong with the request: bad syntax, missing target, state clash, failed rules or too many calls.
400 vs 422: unparseable JSON vs valid JSON that breaks a rule
409: duplicate email or stale version (conflicts with current state)
429: always send `Retry-After` (limits on page 8)

items: Returning `200` with an error in the body
Using 403 when the token is simply missing
Sending 400 for every validation failure
`4xx` means the client should change the request
`5xx` means the server failed, so a retry may work
`Retry-After` tells clients when to try again

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Never leak stack traces in a 500: log them, return a generic error.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: 401 = who are you? 403 = I know you, still no. Full code map on page 14.

blocks.q: Q10. What is a JWT and how is it structured?
a_bullets: A JWT is a signed, self-contained token the server can verify without a database lookup.
Three base64url parts joined by dots: ==header.payload.signature==
Header names the `alg`; payload holds claims like `sub`, `exp`, `aud`
Signature proves it is untampered, not secret: **never** store passwords in it
Verify `alg`, `exp` and `aud` on every request

blocks.q: Q11. What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?
a_bullets: Sessions keep state on the server and send a session ID; tokens carry the state in the token itself.
Session: server looks up `sid` in Redis or DB on each request
Token: server only verifies the signature, so it stays stateless
Sessions revoke instantly; tokens are hard to cancel early
Browsers pair sessions with `HttpOnly` cookies; APIs use Bearer tokens

blocks.q: Q12. How do access tokens and refresh tokens work together?
a_bullets: A short-lived access token calls the API; a long-lived refresh token only gets new access tokens.
Access token lives ~15 minutes, so a leak expires fast
Refresh token goes to the auth server only, never to the API
**Rotate** it on every use and detect reuse of an old one
Store it in an `HttpOnly` cookie, not `localStorage`

blocks.title: Interview line
blocks.text: JWT trades easy scaling for hard revocation. Fix it with short expiry plus refresh rotation.

items: Accepting tokens with `alg: none`
Keeping access tokens valid for days
Putting secrets or PII in the payload

blocks.q: Q13. How do you revoke or invalidate a JWT before it expires?
a_bullets: A stateless JWT cannot be recalled, so you add a small amount of server state to block it.
Denylist the token's `jti` in Redis with a TTL equal to its remaining life
Keep access tokens short and revoke the refresh token instead
Store a per-user `token_version`; bump it on logout or password change
Each check costs a lookup, so only the denylist stays small

blocks.text: Four questions on ==delegated access==: **who** is calling and **what** may they do. Token internals are on the JWT page.

blocks.q: Q14. How does the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow work?
a_bullets: The app sends the user to the auth server, gets a short-lived `code` back, then swaps it for tokens server-side.
The user logs in at the auth server, never at the app
The `state` param blocks CSRF on the redirect
The code is single-use and lives about 60 seconds
The code-for-token swap uses the client secret

blocks.q: Q15. What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 ==authorizes== access to resources. OpenID Connect adds ==authentication== on top, proving who the user is.
OIDC reuses the same flows with scope `openid`
It returns an ID token, a JWT of user claims
`/userinfo` and discovery endpoints are standardised

blocks.q: Q16. Why is PKCE needed and which OAuth grant types exist?
a_bullets: PKCE stops a stolen ==authorization code== being redeemed. Public clients (SPA, mobile) cannot keep a client secret.
The app hashes a random `code_verifier` into a `code_challenge`
The token call must send the original verifier
An attacker holding only the code gets nothing
OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for every code flow

slides.page_title: API Keys, Basic and Bearer Auth

blocks.q: Q17. What is the difference between API keys, Basic auth and Bearer tokens?
a_bullets: An API key identifies the calling ==app==. Basic sends the user's own credentials. A Bearer token is a ==short-lived credential== for whoever holds it.
Basic is base64, which is encoding and not encryption
API keys are long-lived and rarely scoped
Bearer tokens expire and carry scopes
All three need HTTPS

items: Putting tokens or keys in the URL query string
Skipping the `state` check on the redirect
Using implicit flow for a new SPA
Shipping an API key inside a mobile app
Scope every key to least privilege
Hash keys at rest, show them once
Rotate keys on a schedule

blocks.title: Say in the interview
blocks.text: OAuth = delegate access. OIDC = prove identity. PKCE = protect the code.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: For user-facing APIs, pick short-lived Bearer tokens; keep API keys server-side.

slides.subtitle: Q14 to Q17

blocks.q: Q18. What is CORS and how does a preflight request work?
a_bullets: ==CORS== lets a server tell the browser which other origins may read its responses.
Non-simple requests (PUT, custom headers, JSON) trigger an `OPTIONS` **preflight** first.
Server answers with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers; no match, browser blocks.
Enforced by the **browser** only; curl and servers ignore it.
`Max-Age` caches the preflight result, saving round trips.

blocks.q: Q19. What is the difference between CORS and CSRF?
a_bullets: CORS relaxes the same-origin policy; ==CSRF== abuses cookies the browser auto-sends.
CORS protects **reading** responses across origins.
CSRF tricks a logged-in user into **changing** state.
CORS does not stop CSRF: the forged request still reaches the server.
Defend with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, or Bearer headers.

blocks.q: Q20. What are BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities and how do you prevent them?
a_bullets: ==BOLA== (IDOR): user changes an ID and reads someone else's object.
Example: `GET /orders/1002` returns another customer's order.
Check **ownership** on every object access, not just login.
Use unguessable UUIDs as defence in depth, never as the fix.
Return 404, not 403, so IDs cannot be probed.

blocks.q: Q21. How do you prevent SQL injection and mass assignment in an API?
a_bullets: Never concatenate input into SQL; use ==parameterized queries== or an ORM.
Mass assignment: client sets fields like `role` you never meant to expose.
**Allowlist** writable fields; never spread `req.body` into a model.
Use separate input DTOs and schema validation.
Run the DB user with least privilege.

blocks.q: Q22. How do you secure an API in production (HTTPS, headers, validation, secrets)?
a_bullets: Layer defences: ==HTTPS everywhere==, auth, validation, secrets management, monitoring.
Send HSTS and `nosniff` headers; redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Validate every input by schema: type, length, range; reject the rest.
Keep secrets in a vault or env, **never** in Git.
Rate limit, log access, and return generic errors.

items: Allowlist origins, never `*` with credentials
Cap request body size and field lengths
Rotate secrets and audit access logs

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: CORS is not authentication. A wildcard origin with credentials is a real bug.

blocks.title: Defence in depth
blocks.text: Answer with layers: transport, identity, ownership, input, then monitoring.

blocks.q: Q23. What is the difference between offset and cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== skips N rows with `LIMIT/OFFSET`. A ==cursor== resumes after the last row you saw, using an opaque token.
Offset must scan and throw away N rows, so deep pages get **slow**
Rows inserted mid-read make offset pages repeat or skip items
Cursor cost stays flat, but you cannot jump to page N

blocks.q: Q24. How does keyset pagination work in SQL?
a_bullets: Keyset pagination filters with `WHERE` on the last row's sort values, so the database seeks through an index instead of skipping rows.
ORDER BY a unique, indexed key; add `id` as tiebreaker
Index `(created_at, id)` lets the seek jump straight in
Cursor = last row's values, base64-encoded
example_code: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC

blocks.q: Q25. How do you design filtering, sorting and field selection in a REST API?
a_bullets: Use query parameters on the collection: `field=value` filters, `sort=-field` ordering, and `fields=` to trim the response.
==Whitelist== filterable and sortable fields, since unindexed ones cause full scans
Express ranges with suffixes like `_gte` and `_lte`
Cap `limit` (say 100) and add a sort tiebreaker

items: `OFFSET` on a million-row table
Cursor sorted on a non-unique column
No upper bound on `limit`
Exact total count on every request

blocks.title: Say in the interview
blocks.text: Offset for small, jumpable tables. Cursor for feeds and large data.

blocks.q: Q26. How do you return pagination metadata and links (Link header, total count)?
a_bullets: Send navigation as `Link` headers (RFC 8288, rel `next`/`prev`/`first`/`last`) or a `links` object in the body. Treat the ==total count== as optional, because `COUNT(*)` is costly.
Cursor APIs return `next_cursor` and `has_more`, not totals
Offset APIs may add `X-Total-Count` or `meta.total`
Clients should **follow links**, never build URLs themselves

slides.page_title: Rate Limit Algorithms and Cache Patterns

blocks.q: Q27. How do the token bucket and sliding window rate limiting algorithms work?
a_bullets: A ==token bucket== refills tokens at a steady rate and each request spends one. A ==sliding window== counts requests in the last N seconds.
Bucket empty means reject with **429**; bursts up to capacity pass.
Sliding window log stores timestamps: exact but memory-heavy.
Sliding window counter blends two fixed windows: cheap, approximate.

blocks.q: Q28. How do you implement distributed rate limiting with Redis?
a_bullets: Keep counters in a ==shared Redis== so every API node sees one count per client key.
Run check-and-update in one **atomic** Lua script, never GET then SET.
Use `INCR` plus `EXPIRE` for a fixed window.
Use a sorted set (`ZADD`, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`) for a sliding window.

blocks.q: Q30. What are cache-aside, write-through and write-back, and how do you invalidate a cache?
a_bullets: ==Cache-aside== makes the app load from the DB on a miss. ==Write-through== writes cache and DB together. ==Write-back== writes the cache first and the DB later.
Invalidate with a TTL, a delete on write, or event-based purges.
Write-back is fastest but can **lose data** if the cache dies.

blocks.title: Invalidation rule
blocks.text: On write, **delete** the cache key instead of updating it. The next read refills it with fresh data.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Add `Vary: Accept-Encoding` so caches keep one copy per format.

slides.subtitle: Q27 to Q30

blocks.q: Q29. How do ETag and Cache-Control work for HTTP caching?
a_bullets: `Cache-Control` says how long a response stays fresh; `ETag` is a version tag used to revalidate it.
`max-age=60` lets the client reuse it without asking the server.
After expiry, the client sends `If-None-Match` with the stored ETag.
Unchanged data returns **304** with no body, saving bandwidth.

blocks.q: Q31. What is an API gateway and what does it do?
a_bullets: It is the ==single entry point== in front of your backend services. It handles the cross-cutting work so each service doesn't have to.
**Routing**: `/orders/*` goes to the orders service, `/users/*` to the users service
**Auth and limits**: verify the JWT once, then apply per-client rate limits
**Transform and observe**: aggregate responses, cache, log, trace
Trade-off: it can become a bottleneck or a single point of failure

blocks.q: Q32. What is the difference between an API gateway, a reverse proxy and a load balancer?
a_bullets: All three sit in front of servers. They differ in ==how much they understand== about your API.
**Load balancer**: spreads traffic over identical instances, with health checks
**Reverse proxy**: hides servers, terminates TLS, caches and compresses
**Gateway**: a reverse proxy that is API-aware (auth, quotas, routing by route)
Real stacks chain them: LB → gateway → services

items: Business logic creeping into the gateway
One gateway instance with no redundancy
Skipping auth checks on internal routes

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Name the trade-off: a gateway adds one hop of latency, so run it as a redundant cluster.

blocks.title: Say in the interview
blocks.text: Gateway = the front door for APIs. Webhooks push, polling pulls. Verify the signature and dedupe by event ID.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Compare signatures with a constant-time check, and rotate the secret with a grace overlap.

blocks.q: Q33. What is a webhook and how is it different from polling?
a_bullets: A webhook is an ==HTTP callback==. The provider POSTs to your URL when an event happens, so you don't ask repeatedly.
**Polling**: the client calls `GET /status` on a timer, and most calls return nothing
**Webhook**: one push per event, near real-time, far fewer wasted requests
Catch: your endpoint must be public and always available
Payload is a small event, often fetched in full by ID afterwards

blocks.q: Q34. How do you secure webhooks and make delivery reliable?
a_bullets: Prove the sender is genuine with an ==HMAC signature==, and expect at-least-once delivery, so duplicates will arrive.
**Verify**: HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with a shared secret, plus a timestamp to block replays
**Respond fast**: return `2xx` at once, then process the event in a queue
**Dedupe**: store the event ID so a retry is handled only once
**Retry**: exponential backoff, then a dead-letter queue

blocks.q: Q35. How do you make a payment POST endpoint idempotent?
a_bullets: The client sends a unique ==Idempotency-Key== with each payment. The server stores the first result and replays it on any retry.
Save key + request hash + response in a table with a **UNIQUE** key
Same key, different body: reject with `422`
Same key still running: return `409`, never charge twice
Expire keys after about 24 hours

blocks.q: Q36. What are the API versioning strategies and which would you pick?
a_bullets: Four common ways: URI path, header, query parameter, or media type. I pick ==URI path== (`/v1/`) for public APIs because it is visible and easy to route.
Version only on breaking changes, not every release
Header and media-type versions keep URLs clean but are harder to test
Run at most two or three live versions

blocks.q: Q37. How do you handle backward-compatible changes and deprecation?
a_bullets: Only make ==additive== changes inside a version. Announce removals early and give clients a long sunset window.
Never remove, rename or retype a field in place
Clients must ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
Send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers on old versions
Track usage per version, then email the heavy callers

slides.page_title: Large File Uploads and Common Mistakes

blocks.q: Q38. How do you design large file uploads (multipart, presigned URLs, resumable)?
a_bullets: Don't stream big files through your API. Hand out a ==presigned URL== so the client uploads straight to object storage, in chunks.
Multipart: split into 5-100 MB parts, upload in parallel
Presigned URL: short expiry, scoped to one key and size
Resumable: track uploaded parts, retry only the failed ones
Verify with a checksum, then mark the file complete

items: Presign with a short expiry and fixed key
Enforce a max size and content type
Abort and clean up unfinished multiparts
Treating a retried POST as a new payment
Caching idempotency keys only in app memory
Versioning every small change, or none at all
Proxying multi-GB uploads through the API server

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say the API only issues URLs and records metadata; the bytes never touch it.

blocks.title: Link back
blocks.text: Why POST needs a key while PUT and DELETE don't: page 3, safe vs idempotent.

slides.subtitle: Q35 to Q38

blocks.q: Q39. How do you test an API with unit, integration, contract and load tests?
a_bullets: Use a ==test pyramid==: many fast unit tests, fewer integration and contract tests, and a few load tests before release.
**Unit**: one function or handler, with dependencies faked.
**Integration**: real HTTP, real DB, real routing and auth.
**Contract**: consumer and provider agree on the schema.
**Load**: p95 latency and error rate under traffic (k6, JMeter).

blocks.q: Q40. What is the difference between mocking, stubbing and contract testing?
a_bullets: A **stub** returns canned answers; a **mock** also verifies how it was called. ==Contract testing== checks that two services agree on the API shape without running both together.
Stub: replaces a dependency, asserts on the result.
Mock: asserts calls, such as the args or how often.
Contract: the consumer publishes a pact and the provider CI verifies it (Pact).

blocks.q: Q41. What are the key metrics to monitor for an API (RED, latency percentiles)?
a_bullets: Track ==RED==: **R**ate (requests per second), **E**rrors (5xx share) and **D**uration (latency) for every endpoint.
Alert on percentiles, not averages: p50 is typical, p95 and p99 show the slow tail.
Average latency hides the 1% of users who time out.
Add saturation (CPU, pool usage) and set SLO alerts on error rate and p99.

blocks.q: Q42. How do logging, tracing and correlation IDs help debug a production API?
a_bullets: A ==correlation ID== is generated at the edge and passed on every call, so one request's logs can be joined across services.
Logs: structured JSON events say what happened.
Traces: spans show where the time went (OpenTelemetry).
Metrics say something is wrong; logs and traces say why.

blocks.title: Say in the interview
blocks.text: Metrics detect, traces locate, logs explain. Retries and timeouts are covered on page 12.

caption.text:
50 API questions they will ask you in your next backend interview. 🎯

APIs show up in almost every SDE and backend round, and the same questions keep coming back. We boiled them down to the 50 most asked, each with a short direct answer, key points and a visual you can sketch from memory.

What's inside the carousel:

📌 REST and HTTP basics
📌 Methods and status codes
📌 JWT and sessions
📌 OAuth 2.0 and API keys
📌 CORS and API security
📌 Pagination and filtering
📌 Rate limiting and caching
📌 API gateway and webhooks
📌 Idempotency, versioning and file uploads
📌 Testing and monitoring
📌 Scalability and performance
📌 Real-world API design scenarios
📌 A final API interview cheatsheet

Swipe through, save it for your prep, and send it to the friend who has an interview coming up. 🔖

Now be honest: which API question do you find the hardest? Idempotency? OAuth flows? Designing rate limiting? Tell us in the comments. 👇
